growth_story.headline: After a 1990s collapse and a remittance-fed 2000s boom, Moldova has grown slower and less steadily since 2009, yet income per person is the highest since 1990.
growth_story.arc: Income per person shrank by 10.1 percent a year on average from 1991 to 1999. Independence ended Soviet energy subsidies and guaranteed markets, the defense industries collapsed, the Transnistria region broke away, and Russia's 1998 crisis cut short a brief recovery. From 2000 to 2008 it grew 6.2 percent a year, as many workers left for jobs abroad and sent money home, and as farms grew more productive, workers moved out of farming into low-skill manufacturing and services. Since 2009 growth has slowed to 3.6 percent a year and swung hard, with falls in 2009, 2012, 2020 and 2022, a near-stall after the 2014 bank fraud, and a jump of 15.7 percent in 2021. The World Bank says the old growth model has increasingly failed to raise productivity, money from workers abroad has declined since its 2007 peak, and emigration and ageing have shrunk the workforce. Even so, growth over 2016 to 2025 averaged 4.0 percent a year, a little above the 3.8 of 2006 to 2015, and income per person rose back above its 1990 level in 2023 and reached its highest level since 1990 in 2025.

threads.title: Post-Soviet collapse
threads.text: Independence ended cheap Soviet energy and guaranteed Soviet markets, the defense industries collapsed, and the breakaway Transnistria region took much of the country's modern industry and most of its power plant capacity. Growth turned positive in 1997, but Russia's 1998 financial crisis cut that recovery short.

threads.title: Remittances rose, then faded
threads.text: By the early 2000s rural poverty had pushed many Moldovans to work abroad, and the money they sent home became a major source of household income and spending. The World Bank says these flows have declined steadily since their 2007 peak, and links this to slower growth after 2009.

threads.title: The 2014 bank fraud
threads.text: In late 2014 a large fraud was exposed in the banking system, and three banks were closed at great public cost. Confidence collapsed and donor money largely froze, and income per person grew only 0.4 percent in 2015.

threads.title: Shocks in quick succession
threads.text: Since 2020 the pandemic, severe droughts, Russia's war in Ukraine and an energy crisis have hit one after another, so income per person fell 7.3 percent in 2020, rose 15.7 percent in 2021 and fell 2.1 percent in 2022. In early 2025 a severe energy crisis, after Russian gas stopped flowing through Ukraine, stalled the economy again.

since_last_year.text: After the energy crisis stalled the economy in early 2025, a better-than-expected harvest and more spending by households and firms brought a recovery later in the year, and income per person grew 4.2 percent in 2025. In 2026 the conflict in the Middle East pushed energy prices and inflation up again. The World Bank reports that growth slowed sharply in the first half of 2026 and expects a weaker year than 2025.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says Moldova's growth has lagged other EU candidates, and the IMF and World Bank describe total output barely growing in 2024 and recovering in 2025. Yet in the data income per person grew 2.6 percent in 2024 and 4.2 percent in 2025, and is at its highest since 1990. Much of the gap is the shrinking population the sources describe: with steady emigration, slow growth in total output becomes faster growth in income per person.
